title: MTTD and MTTR
summary: Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond are the two headline measures of security operations performance. Mean Time to Detect measures the elapsed interval between when malicious activity actually began and when it was first identified, while Mean Time to Respond measures the interval from identification to containment or resolution, depending on how the organisation defines the endpoint. Both are averages and both are therefore easily misread. A mean computed over a handful of incidents is dominated by outliers, so distributions, medians and percentiles communicate far more than a single number. The definitions themselves are the hardest part. Detection time cannot be measured from the alert timestamp unless you also determine when the activity started, which usually requires retrospective log analysis and often moves the start earlier once the incident is understood. Response end is equally ambiguous: is it containment of the immediate threat, eradication, restoration of service, or case closure. Without a written definition agreed with the business, teams optimise a metric they cannot compare over time. The measures are also gameable. Suppressing noisy detections lowers alert volume and can appear to improve response time while degrading detection. Closing cases quickly without corroboration improves the average and hides unresolved risk. The genuinely useful approach is to pair times with quality measures: the proportion of incidents found by internal detection rather than external notification, the fraction detected at each ATT&CK stage, dwell time distributions, and containment precision. Tracking MTTD and MTTR by incident class and detection source, and reviewing the specific incidents that set the extremes, converts an executive number into an engineering feedback loop.
objectives: You will be able to define detection start, detection point, containment and closure precisely enough that the metric is comparable over time.
You will be able to explain why means alone mislead and use medians, percentiles and distributions when reporting response performance.
You will be able to compute dwell time for an incident by reconstructing the true start of activity from retrospective log evidence.
You will be able to identify how suppressing alerts or closing cases prematurely can artificially improve these metrics.
You will be able to complement timing metrics with detection-source and coverage-quality measures such as internal versus external discovery.
You will be able to segment MTTD and MTTR by incident class and use the worst cases to drive specific detection or playbook improvements.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: Mean Time to Detect is the average time between an attack starting and your team noticing it. Mean Time to Respond is the average time from noticing it to containing it. Together they are the two headline numbers for how well a security team performs. Mean simply means average.
beginner.whyItMatters: These numbers tell leadership whether the security team is getting faster or slower. They also show where the weak points are. A slow detection time means your sensors or rules are missing things. A slow response time usually means your procedures are unclear. Without measuring, you are guessing about your own readiness.
howItWorks: First, agree on exactly when the clock starts. Usually that is when the attack began.
Then agree on when detection counts, such as when an analyst confirms the alert.
Agree on exactly when response ends: containment, full cleanup, or case closure.
For each incident, record those three timestamps and subtract them to get durations.
Average the durations, but also look at the median and the worst cases.
Finally, review the slowest incidents to find the specific step that failed.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital tracking how long patients wait. The average wait looks fine, but one patient waited nine hours and that single case hides the truth. So the hospital also reports the longest waits and the middle value. Security metrics behave the same way. One very slow incident can make an average look terrible, and one very fast incident can make it look falsely good.
takeaways: An average alone hides the story; check the median and worst cases.
Write down your definitions, or the numbers cannot be compared over time.
Watch for teams that improve the number by closing cases early.
